title: The supplement of spermidine attenuates high-fat diet-induced hepatic lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and inflammation in large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea)

sections.abstract: Prolonged high-fat diet (HFD) provokes hepatic lipid deposition and injury in farmed fish, highlighting an urgent need for effective mitigation strategies. As a natural polyamine, spermidine (SP) has been demonstrated to improve hepatic lipid accumulation and damage in mammals, but its role in fish liver health remains unknown. In this study, juvenile large yellow croakers (Larmichthys crocea) were fed with control diet (CON), HFD, or HFD containing 0.02 %SP, 0.1 %SP, and 0.5 %SP. After 8 weeks, the results exhibited that the SP supplement did not significantly influence the survival, growth performance, and body composition of croakers. However, 0.1 %SP addition reduced the hepatosomatic index of croakers fed HFD. Moreover, SP addition attenuated HFD-induced elevations in hepatic and serum triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol levels. Meanwhile, SP supplementation significantly suppressed HFD-driven upregulation of lipogenic genes and attenuated HFD-mediated downregulation of autophagy-related genes at the transcriptional level. Notably, SP addition significantly stimulated hepatic AMPK pathway activation in croakers fed HFD. Furthermore, 0.1 %SP addition enhanced hepatic superoxide dismutase and catalase activities while reducing malondialdehyde levels in croakers fed HFD. Simultaneously, SP addition ameliorated HFD-elevated activities of alanine transaminase and aspartate transaminase, and inhibited HFD-triggered transcriptions of hepatic proinflammatory genes. Consistently, SP treatment in vitro efficiently alleviated palmitic acid-triggered lipid deposition and inflammatory responses in croaker hepatocytes. Collectively, 0.1 %SP supplement could attenuate HFD-induced hepatic lipid accumulation, oxidative stress, and inflammation in croaker, and these improvements may be attributed to the activation of AMPK pathway and autophagy.
